Aetosauria.note: Armoured, pig-snouted herbivorous archosaurs common in northern Triassic red beds; extinct at the end-Triassic mass extinction.
Aetosauria.conf_note: PBDB's EXTANT/lad=0 tag is a database error - no aetosaur is known past the end-Triassic. pbdb_raw's 119.57 Ma bound is also spurious; the group is exclusively Triassic.

Allosaurus.note: The dominant Morrison predator, known from dozens of individuals at the Cleveland-Lloyd quarry.

Anchiornis.note: A small feathered paravian preserved well enough for its actual colour pattern to be reconstructed from melanosomes.

Anhanguera.note: A crested, toothed fishing pterosaur from Brazil's Santana Formation, known from beautifully preserved three-dimensional skulls that reveal the shape of its bony head crest.

Antarctopelta.note: The first ankylosaur from Antarctica, from the James Ross Basin of the still-forested Cretaceous continent.

Archelon.note: A four-metre sea turtle, the largest ever, cruising the warm inland sea.

Argentinosaurus.note: A titanosaur among the largest land animals ever, from the Cretaceous of Patagonia.

Brachiosaurus.note: A sauropod holding its neck high above the canopy, weighing perhaps thirty tonnes; the similar Tendaguru animal from Africa is now placed in its own genus, Giraffatitan.
Brachiosaurus.hb: high browser with forelimbs longer than hindlimbs

Carbonemys.note: A car-sized side-necked turtle sharing Titanoboa's steamy post-impact wetlands.

Carcharodontosaurus.note: A shark-toothed giant predator of the mid-Cretaceous North African floodplains.

Carnotaurus.note: A horned, tiny-armed abelisaur theropod endemic to Cretaceous South America.

Cetiosaurus.note: An early large sauropod, originally mistaken for a giant marine reptile.
Cetiosaurus.conf_note: Valid Cetiosaurus material caps out in the Callovian; the Early Cretaceous tail in PBDB's robust bin reflects indeterminate sauropod fragments loosely assigned to the genus.

Chaohusaurus.note: One of the earliest ichthyosaurs: within a few million years of the extinction, reptiles are already back in the sea.

Coelophysis.note: A slender early theropod dinosaur, hundreds found together at Ghost Ranch in Pangaea's western deserts.

Coelophysis bauri.note: A slender early theropod known from hundreds of individuals at Ghost Ranch, piled up in a single mass death assemblage.

Compsognathus.note: A chicken-sized coelurosaur dinosaur washed into the lagoon, its last meal a lizard in its gut.

Cryolophosaurus ellioti.note: A crested theropod from the Transantarctic Mountains, showing dinosaurs living at high southern latitudes.

Desmatosuchus.note: A spike-shouldered aetosaur from the Late Triassic American Southwest, armoured along back and flanks and rooting through the soil with a pig-like snout.

Dilophosaurus.note: A crested early theropod, six metres long and nothing like its film portrayal.

Edmontosaurus.note: A duck-billed hadrosaur that grazed the coastal plains beside the retreating Interior Seaway.

Eudimorphodon.note: An early pterosaur with a complex tooth battery, already fully capable of powered flight.

Giganotosaurus.note: A giant carcharodontosaur, rivalling T. rex in size, hunting the Patagonian titanosaurs.

Giraffatitan.note: A towering sauropod from Tanzania's Tendaguru beds, long described as an African species of Brachiosaurus before differences in its skull and proportions placed it in its own genus.

Gryposuchus.note: A slender-snouted gharial up to ten metres long, a specialised fish-eater sharing the water with the giant caimans.

Guanlong.note: An early crested tyrannosauroid from the Jurassic of Xinjiang, small and long-armed, 90 million years before T. rex.

Hatzegopteryx.note: A giraffe-sized pterosaur from the Cretaceous island of Hateg in what is now Romania, apex predator of a dwarf-dinosaur fauna.

Hylonomus.note: One of the first true reptiles, sheltering in hollow lycophyte stumps in Nova Scotia.
Hylonomus.hb: insectivore living in hollow lycopsid stumps

Hylonomus lyelli.note: A lizard-shaped animal found inside fossil tree stumps at Joggins, and the earliest well-established amniote.

Ichthyosauria.note: Dolphin-shaped marine reptiles, from one to over twenty metres, bearing live young at sea from the Early Triassic on.

Ichthyosaurus.note: Streamlined, live-bearing marine reptiles; Mary Anning's Lyme Regis specimens are how the world learned they existed.
Ichthyosaurus.conf_note: The true genus Ichthyosaurus (type species I. communis) is a Hettangian-Pliensbachian English/west European taxon; PBDB's wider bin and na-w/sa-s occurrences reflect 19th-century material since reassigned to other ichthyosaur genera.

Iguanodon.note: A large ornithopod with a thumb spike, and one of the first dinosaurs recognised as such.

Isisaurus.note: A titanosaur of latest-Cretaceous India whose nesting grounds are preserved as fossil egg clutches.

Keichousaurus.note: A small long-necked marine reptile found by the thousand in Guizhou Triassic shales.

Kronosaurus.note: A giant short-necked pliosaur, apex predator of the cold Cretaceous sea over central Australia.

Liopleurodon.note: A short-necked pliosaur with a skull well over a metre long, hunting other marine reptiles.
Liopleurodon.conf_note: Diagnostic Liopleurodon ferox material is Callovian, France/England. Popular reconstructions (and PBDB's wider bin) inflate it with younger pliosaurid material historically misassigned to the genus.

Mamenchisaurus.note: A Chinese sauropod with a neck half its total length -- among the longest necks any animal has had.

Massospondylus.note: An early sauropodomorph from South African Jurassic red beds, known even from embryos in the egg.

Megalosaurus.note: The first dinosaur ever formally named, from Oxfordshire, decades before anyone had the concept of a dinosaur.
Megalosaurus.conf_note: Diagnostic Megalosaurus bucklandii material is Bathonian, Oxfordshire only. Megalosaurus is the archetypal 19th-century wastebasket theropod genus; the wider PBDB bin and as-c occurrence reflect fragments elsewhere once dumped under the name.

Mesosaurus.note: A small aquatic reptile of Permian Gondwanan lakes, found on matching shores in Brazil and South Africa - Wegener's evidence for drift.

Microraptor.note: A four-winged dromaeosaur with flight feathers on both fore and hind limbs, glossy black in life.

Morrosaurus.note: A small ornithopod of the high-latitude Cretaceous forests of the Antarctic Peninsula.

Mosasauridae.note: Giant marine lizards, relatives of monitors and snakes, that took the top-predator role in every Late Cretaceous sea.

Mosasaurus.note: A giant marine lizard, related to monitors and snakes, that takes over the sea in the last twenty million years of the era.

Mourasuchus.note: A bizarre caiman with a long, flat, duck-like snout, probably a filter-feeder straining small prey from the water.

Nothosaurus.note: A long-necked, semi-aquatic fish-catcher representing an early stage of the sauropterygian move into the sea.

Ornithocheiridae.note: Large fish-eating pterosaurs patrolling Cretaceous coastlines.

Ouranosaurus.note: A sail-backed iguanodont sharing the lush Cretaceous river deltas of what is now the desert.

Paralititan.note: A colossal titanosaur from the mangrove coasts of Late Cretaceous Egypt (Bahariya).

Pareiasauria.note: Bulky armoured herbivorous reptiles, the cattle of the terminal Permian landscape.

Phytosauria.note: Crocodile-shaped archosaurs lurking in Late Triassic rivers before crocodiles proper existed.

Placodontia.note: Marine reptiles with flat crushing teeth and, in some, turtle-like armour, specialised on shellfish.

Placodus.note: A Triassic placodont with peg-like front teeth and flat crushing cheek teeth, foraging on shellfish in the shallow Germanic Basin sea without the shell-like armour of its later relatives.

Plateosaurus.note: An early long-necked sauropodomorph, and among the first genuinely large herbivorous dinosaurs.

Platypterygius.note: A large, late ichthyosaur found world-wide in Early Cretaceous seas; some Australian specimens are preserved as opal.

Plesiosauria.note: Long-necked, four-flippered marine reptiles that 'flew' underwater, from coastal forms to open-ocean giants.

Plesiosaurus.note: Long-necked, four-flippered marine reptiles rowing through shallow Jurassic seas.
Plesiosaurus.conf_note: Genus Plesiosaurus (P. dolichodeirus) is restricted to the Hettangian-Sinemurian of England. It is history's classic wastebasket plesiosaur name; the Cretaceous tail in PBDB's bin is old material long since moved to other genera.

Postosuchus.note: A large pseudosuchian predator that outranked every dinosaur of its day, and died out at the boundary.

Proterosuchus.note: An early archosaur, sprawling and crocodile-like, at the root of the lineage that will produce dinosaurs and birds.

Protoceratops.note: The Gobi ceratopsian found with nests and eggs, and probably the origin of the griffin legend.

Psittacosaurus.note: A parrot-beaked early ceratopsian, the most abundant dinosaur of the Jehol beds.

Pterodactylus.note: A small short-tailed pterosaur from Solnhofen, and the first pterosaur ever described.

Purussaurus.note: A giant caiman over ten metres long, ruling the vast Pebas wetland of Miocene Amazonia.

Quetzalcoatlus.note: A pterosaur the size of a small aircraft, standing as tall as a giraffe and probably foraging on foot.
Quetzalcoatlus.hb: terrestrial stalker and soaring flier, ~11 m wingspan

Rajasaurus.note: A horned abelisaur theropod from the Lameta beds, hunting amid the erupting Deccan Traps.

Rhamphorhynchus.note: A long-tailed pterosaur of the same lagoons, some specimens preserving the wing membrane and throat pouch.

Rukwatitan.note: A titanosaur from the East African rift sediments, part of a distinct southern fauna.

Rutiodon.note: A slender, long-snouted phytosaur from the Late Triassic of the eastern United States, crocodile-like in build though unrelated, with nostrils set back near the eyes rather than the snout tip.

Scelidosaurus.note: An early armoured dinosaur, at the base of the lineage leading to stegosaurs and ankylosaurs.

Scutosaurus.note: A heavily built pareiasaur from the Russian Permian, knobbly-skulled and barrel-bodied.

Shonisaurus.note: A giant ichthyosaur reaching twenty metres, comparable to a modern large whale.

Sinosauropteryx.note: The first dinosaur found with unambiguous filamentous feathers, and later with its ginger-and-white banded tail decoded.

Spinosaurus.note: A sail-backed, semi-aquatic theropod larger than T. rex, from the Kem Kem rivers of the Sahara.

Spinosaurus aegyptiacus.note: A sail-backed, paddle-tailed theropod that hunted fish in North African river systems.

Stegosaurus.note: Plated, spike-tailed, and with a brain famously small relative to its bulk.
Stegosaurus.hb: low browser with dorsal plates and a spiked tail

Stupendemys.note: The largest freshwater turtle ever, a side-neck with a shell over three metres across and horns on the front of it.

Tanystropheus.note: A reptile whose neck is longer than the rest of it combined, with only twelve vertebrae in it.

Tarbosaurus.note: The Asian giant tyrannosaur of the Nemegt Formation, close kin to T. rex and nearly as large.

Titanoboa.note: A 13-metre snake from the Paleocene Cerrejon rainforest of Colombia - the largest snake known.

Titanoboa cerrejonensis.note: A thirteen-metre, tonne-weight constrictor whose bulk is itself a thermometer for Paleocene tropical heat.

Triceratops.note: A horned, frilled ceratopsian and one of the most abundant large animals in the final Cretaceous ecosystems.
Triceratops.hb: low browser with a frill and three horns

Tylosaurus.note: A mosasaur over twelve metres long, the apex predator of the seaway that split North America.

Tyrannosaurus rex.note: Twelve metres, bone-crushing bite, binocular vision, and among the last non-avian dinosaurs to exist.

Varanus priscus.note: A seven-metre monitor lizard, Australia's largest terrestrial predator until the megafauna extinction.

Velociraptor.note: Turkey-sized and feathered, from the Gobi -- one specimen locked in combat with a Protoceratops, both buried by a collapsing dune.

Vulcanodon.note: One of the earliest true sauropods, from Zimbabwe, as Gondwana begins to break apart.
